820.title: Mata Sahib Kaur, mother of the Khalsa
820.hook: at amrit, Sikhs are told Mata Sahib Kaur is their spiritual mother
820.howItsDone: At an amrit ceremony, the new initiates are told that their spiritual father is Guru Gobind Singh, their spiritual mother is Mata Sahib Kaur, and their home is Anandpur Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Sundari, sending letters of counsel out of Delhi to a scattered people. Your line: she led. A new week starts today, with a mother.

Who are your parents? Most days that's a simple question. But at a Sikh amrit ceremony, once the new initiates have taken the amrit, they are given a second family on top of the one they were born into. They are told who their spiritual father is, who their spiritual mother is, and where their spiritual home is. People come to that moment from every kind of family. Some have lost a mother. Some never knew one. Some have a wonderful one. And all of them, standing together, are handed the same name. Today: Anandpur.
screen: `WHO ARE YOUR PARENTS?` → `A SECOND FAMILY AT AMRIT.` → `ONE MOTHER FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Mata Sahib Kaur was a wife of Guru Gobind Singh. Tradition says she had no children of her own, and that the Guru told her she would be the mother of a much larger family: the Khalsa. That is how Sikhs remember her. At amrit, the new members of the Khalsa are told: your father is Guru Gobind Singh, your mother is Mata Sahib Kaur, and your home is Anandpur. A shopkeeper's son and a farmer's daughter, people whose families might never have shared a meal, walk out of the ceremony as brothers and sisters, with the same mother. The family is not made by blood. It's made by the bowl. Two days ago, with Mata Jito, we heard that some tellings say it was Mata Sahib Kaur who added the sweets to the first amrit. Either way, the tellings put a woman's hand in that first bowl. After the Guru's death she lived in Delhi beside Mata Sundari, and tradition says she, too, sent letters of guidance to the sangats. Here is the quiet surprise in her story. A woman with no children of her own is remembered as mother to every member of the Khalsa. Being a mother, in this telling, is not only about giving birth. It's about who you hold, who you claim, who you treat as yours. And every time a new Sikh takes amrit, her name is said again.

821.title: Bhai Daya Singh
821.hook: the first to rise at Anandpur, who later, tradition says, carried the Zafarnama
821.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Daya Singh as the first of the Panj Pyare in the Vaisakhi story, and the Zafarnama is read and discussed in Sikh gatherings and schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anandpur, the home named at every amrit. Your line: mother of the khalsa. Today, the man who stood up first.

Every room has that silence. A teacher asks for a volunteer, a manager asks who'll take the hard job, and nobody moves. Everyone looks at their shoes and waits for someone else. Now make it a hillside at Anandpur, a great crowd, and a Guru with a drawn sword asking for a head. The silence must have been enormous. Then one man stands up. He doesn't know what's in the tent. He doesn't know that four more will follow him. He just rises, first, alone. Today: Bhai Daya Singh.
screen: `NOBODY MOVES.` → `A SWORD, AND A HARD QUESTION.` → `ONE MAN STANDS.`

segments.voice: Before that day he was Daya Ram, and tradition says he came from Lahore. When Guru Gobind Singh called for someone ready to give his head, he answered first. He walked into the tent. Four others followed, one at a time. And all five walked out again, the Panj Pyare, the five beloved, the first members of the Khalsa. Daya Ram became Daya Singh. Being first is a strange gift. The second person to stand up still has to be brave. But the first stands into total uncertainty, with no one ahead of him to show it can be survived. Sikhs remember Bhai Daya Singh for that rising, and his story didn't end there. He stayed close to the Guru through the hard years that followed. Then, tradition says, the Guru wrote a letter in Persian verse to the emperor Aurangzeb, a letter Sikhs call the Zafarnama. It names wrongs done to the Guru and his Sikhs, and it speaks of God and of broken promises. Someone had to carry it across a great distance, toward the emperor in the south. Tradition says that was Bhai Daya Singh. Set the two moments side by side. The first time, he rose from a crowd to face a sword. The second time, he rode toward an emperor's court with a letter that accused that court of breaking its word. Both times, someone had to go first, and it was him. Bhai is a title of respect, brother. He's remembered as the brother who stood up before anyone else did.

822.title: The rest of the five
822.hook: Dharam Singh survived the Guru; Himmat, Mohkam and Sahib Singh fell at Chamkaur
822.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Panj Pyare in Ardas, and at an amrit ceremony five initiated Sikhs serve as the Panj Pyare to prepare and give the amrit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Daya Singh, who stood up first when nobody else would. Your line: first to rise. Today, the four who came after him.

Team photos shrink in memory. Years later, people remember the captain, the one who scored, the one who gave the speech. The rest blur into the back row. The Panj Pyare could easily have gone that way: one famous first volunteer, then four others who followed. But Sikhs don't let them blur. They say all five names. They tell where each one came from and how each one's life ended. So today, after the man who stood first, the rest of the five.
screen: `THE BACK ROW BLURS.` → `ONE FAMOUS, FOUR FORGOTTEN?` → `SIKHS SAY ALL FIVE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Dharam Singh, Himmat Singh, Mohkam Singh, Sahib Singh. Tradition says they came from far-flung places and different trades: a farmer, a water-carrier, a washerman, a barber. Men who, in the world around them, would not have eaten at one table. On the day the Khalsa began, each rose after Daya Ram and walked into the tent, one at a time. After that day, their lives went in two directions. Bhai Dharam Singh lived on. Tradition says he stayed with the Guru through the worst of what came, and was still at his side when the Guru traveled south, near the end of his life. He outlived the Guru. The other three did not. When the Guru's small band was surrounded at Chamkaur, Himmat Singh, Mohkam Singh and Sahib Singh were among the Sikhs inside the mud walls. Tradition says they went out to fight, and fell there. Three of the five beloved gave their lives in one place. Some of the five are remembered for how they lived on and kept serving, some for how they died. The tradition doesn't rank them. It puts them side by side, the way they stood when they came out of the tent. The Sikh prayer called Ardas, said at the end of gatherings and daily prayers, remembers the five beloved. And at every amrit ceremony, five Sikhs stand in their place to prepare the amrit. The five keep coming back, as five. Remembering someone by name is a small thing. But it is how the back row gets out of the blur.

823.title: Bhai Sangat Singh
823.hook: tradition says a Sikh who looked like the Guru wore his plume at Chamkaur so the Guru could slip away
823.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Sangat Singh in remembrances of Chamkaur, especially in December when the martyrdoms of that season are recalled, and the gurdwara at Chamkaur keeps the memory of those who fell there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Panj Pyare: Dharam Singh, who lived on, and three who fell at Chamkaur. Your line: the five, remembered. Today, we stay at Chamkaur one more night.

Night at Chamkaur. The mud-walled house is ringed by an army that will attack again at first light. Inside, only a handful of Sikhs are left. They have told the Guru he must go, so the community will not lose him, and the Guru has agreed. But an army watches a house like this. If the Guru's tall plume disappears from the wall, they'll know. Someone has to stay behind and be seen: someone who, in the dark and at a distance, could pass for him. Today: Bhai Sangat Singh.
screen: `NIGHT, AND AN ARMY OUTSIDE.` → `THE GURU MUST GO.` → `SOMEONE MUST BE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Bhai Sangat Singh looked like Guru Gobind Singh, close enough in look and build that, from below, in poor light, he could be taken for him. So before the Guru left, he gave Sangat Singh his own plume, the kalgi, a jeweled ornament worn on the turban, along with his garments. Sangat Singh put them on and took the Guru's place in the house, where the enemy could see him. Then, in the dark, the Guru slipped out with a few companions. When morning came, the army attacked again, believing the Guru was inside. Sangat Singh and the Sikhs with him fought until they fell. Tradition says the enemy at first thought they had killed the Guru himself. It wasn't a trick for its own sake. It was a gift of time. Every hour the soldiers spent watching the plume on the wall was an hour the Guru was further away. Sangat Singh wasn't taking the Guru's honor. He was taking the Guru's danger. Some tellings give part of this story to another Sikh, Bhai Sant Singh, and some speak of the two together. The details shift between tellings, but the shape stays the same: a Sikh who put on what marked the Guru, and stood where the Guru would have stood, so the Guru could live. Sikhs call his name with love, not for looking like the Guru, but for what he did with that likeness.

segments.voice: This isn't about lying for anyone; it's about stepping into a hard spot so someone else can get through. Think of someone near you who's carrying too much right now, a coworker who's behind, a parent who hasn't had a night off, and ask what you could take on so they could step away for a while. Let one thing come: a shift, a dinner, a phone call.

824.title: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan
824.hook: two Pathan brothers carried the Guru in disguise as a holy man through enemy lines
824.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan in tellings of the Guru's escape after Chamkaur, and the story is told at Machhiwara, where the memory of the Guru's stay is kept.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Sangat Singh, wearing the Guru's plume so the Guru could slip away from Chamkaur. Your line: he took his place. Today, where the Guru went next.

A road patrolled by soldiers. Coming down it, a palanquin, a covered seat carried on poles, with a holy man inside dressed in blue. Two Pathan men are carrying it, with a few others walking alongside. The soldiers stop them. Who's this? A holy man, the brothers say, a pir, on his way. They are calm. They are Muslims, telling the soldiers what soldiers would expect to hear. And inside the palanquin sits the man those soldiers are hunting: Guru Gobind Singh. Today: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan.
screen: `A PALANQUIN ON A WATCHED ROAD.` → `A HOLY MAN IN BLUE.` → `THE GURU INSIDE.`

segments.voice: After Chamkaur, the Guru made his way through the night, alone for a time, to the forest near Machhiwara. Tradition says that's where a few of his Sikhs found him again, and where help came from an unexpected direction. Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan were Pathan brothers, horse dealers, who tradition says had sold horses to the Guru in better days and knew him. Now he was a hunted man, and helping him was dangerous. They helped anyway. Their plan was a disguise. The Guru would be dressed in blue robes, as a Muslim holy man, a pir. Tradition says they called him the Pir of Uch, a holy man from a faraway town. They lifted him in a palanquin and carried him on their shoulders through countryside where soldiers were searching. When questioned, they held to their story. If the soldiers had seen through it, the brothers could have paid with their lives. They weren't Sikhs. No one could have demanded this of them. They had known him, they trusted him, and when his life was in danger they put their own on the line. When they parted, tradition says, the Guru gave them a hukamnama, a letter thanking them, so their service would be remembered. And it is. Sikhs tell this story with deep gratitude, in the same thread as Pir Budhu Shah a few days ago and the Nawab of Malerkotla, whom we'll meet soon. Brothers of another faith, carrying the Guru on their shoulders.

825.title: Bhai Moti Ram Mehra
825.hook: tradition says a cook brought warm milk to Mata Gujri and the boys in the cold tower, and later paid with his life
825.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Moti Ram Mehra during the December remembrances of the Sahibzade at Fatehgarh Sahib near Sirhind, where a gurdwara honors him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, carrying the Guru past the soldiers as a holy man in blue. Your line: brothers of another faith. Today, Sirhind, and a gentler courage.

A clay cup of milk, still warm. Not a sword, not a speech, not a rescue. Just a cup of milk, carried at night up to a tower where the winter wind comes straight through. Sikhs tell a heavy story about Sirhind, about Mata Gujri and her two young grandsons held there in the cold, and we've told it gently before. Today we look at it from the side, from the kitchen, through the eyes of one man who couldn't stop what was happening but could still do one warm thing. Today: Bhai Moti Ram Mehra.
screen: `A CUP OF WARM MILK.` → `CARRIED UP AT NIGHT.` → `ONE WARM THING.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Moti Ram Mehra worked in a kitchen at Sirhind, where Mata Gujri and the two younger Sahibzade were held in the cold tower, the Thanda Burj. He was not a soldier. He had no power to open a door. He was a cook. When he learned who was in that tower, and that they were cold and without proper food, he did the one thing a cook can do. He brought them milk. Tradition says he had to get past the guards, and that he gave them what he had so they would let him through. At night he carried warm milk up to a grandmother and two small boys, and they drank it. It changed nothing about the governor's decision. The boys still faced the court, and the story ends the way Sikhs remember it ending; we won't retell that today. But for those nights, in that tower, someone brought something warm. Then it was discovered. Tradition says that for this act, Moti Ram Mehra paid with his life, and his family with him. Sikhs honor him as a martyr, and a gurdwara near Sirhind keeps his name. Not everyone gets to stop an injustice. Not everyone is the governor, or the army, or the hero at the gate. Most of us are closer to the kitchen. His story says what a small, warm act can mean when it's done at a cost, for people the world has decided to leave in the cold. That's why Sikhs put a cook's name beside the martyrs.

826.title: The Nawab of Malerkotla
826.hook: Sher Muhammad Khan protested the execution of the Sahibzade, and Sikhs have honored Malerkotla ever since
826.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Nawab of Malerkotla's protest whenever the story of the Sahibzade is told, especially in the December remembrances, and speak of the town of Malerkotla with gratitude.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Moti Ram Mehra, the cook who carried warm milk up the cold tower. Your line: milk in the cold tower. Today, the same town, and a voice raised in the governor's court.

Sirhind, the governor's court. Two small boys stand before Wazir Khan. The sentence is about to be spoken, and the men around the governor can see where it is going. To object now is to take the wrong side of the man in charge, in public, with your name attached. One of the men in that court is a Muslim nobleman, a guest there, with every reason to keep quiet. He speaks instead. Today: the Nawab of Malerkotla.
screen: `TWO BOYS BEFORE THE GOVERNOR.` → `EVERY REASON TO KEEP QUIET.` → `ONE VOICE OBJECTS.`

segments.voice: His name was Sher Muhammad Khan, the Nawab, the ruler, of a small state called Malerkotla. Tradition says he was present at Sirhind when the governor, Wazir Khan, was deciding what to do with Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, the Guru's younger sons. He was not a friend of the Guru. Tradition even says he had fought against the Guru's forces. And still, when the sentence of death was spoken, he protested. The boys were children, he said, and children must not be punished for what their father had done. Sikhs call his protest the haa da naara, the cry of protest against injustice. Here is the hard part. It didn't work. The governor went ahead. The boys were killed. The Nawab could not save them. So why do Sikhs remember him with such honor? Sikh memory doesn't measure speaking up only by whether it wins. He told the truth in a room that didn't want to hear it, at a cost to himself, for children of another faith. Tradition says that when Guru Gobind Singh heard what the Nawab had done, he blessed him and his town, and Sikhs have honored Malerkotla ever since. Set him beside yesterday's cook. Two people at Sirhind, a Muslim noble in the court and a cook in the kitchen, who could not change the sentence and still did not look away. One carried something warm up the stairs. The other said, out loud, in front of the governor, that children must not be punished.

segments.voice: Think of a room you'll be in soon, a meeting, a family table, where someone without much power gets talked about or decided about: a new employee, a kid, someone who isn't there. Find the one simple sentence you could say, the way the Nawab's was simple: that isn't fair, or let's hear their side. Rehearse it once, quietly, on an out-breath.
